short: One slot of the HashMap's internal array. Every key whose index is that slot ends up in this bucket.
more: The JDK source calls it a "bin". A bucket holds nothing, one node, a chain of nodes, or a tree.

short: The internal array of buckets (Node<K,V>[] table). Its length is always a power of two.
more: Created lazily on the first put.

short: One key-value entry inside a bucket. Stores the key, the value, the key's hash and a pointer to the next node in the chain.
more: Roughly 32 bytes per entry on a 64-bit JVM with compressed pointers, not counting the key and value objects themselves.

short: A number computed from a key. HashMap uses it to decide which bucket the key belongs to.
more: Inside HashMap the "hash" is hashCode() after the high bits have been mixed in: h ^ (h >>> 16).

short: A method on every Java object that returns a 32-bit int summarising the object's contents. HashMap calls it on every key.
more: Equal objects must return equal hash codes. Different objects may share a hash code (a collision).

short: The method that decides whether two objects count as the same. HashMap calls it only after the hash codes match.
more: Default Object.equals compares identity (==). Override it together with hashCode.

short: The rules every hashCode()/equals() pair must obey, most importantly: if a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode().
more: Break it and a HashMap can "lose" entries it still holds.

short: Two different keys that land in the same bucket.
more: Unavoidable: there are about 4 billion possible hash codes but only a handful of buckets. HashMap resolves them by chaining.

short: Collision strategy where each bucket holds a linked list (a "chain") of all the entries that share it.
more: The alternative is open addressing, used by IdentityHashMap, where a colliding entry is placed in another free slot.

short: Collision strategy where a colliding entry is stored in some other free slot of the same array instead of in a list.
more: Used by IdentityHashMap in the JDK (linear probing).

short: A sequence of nodes where each node points to the next. Finding an item means walking from the front: O(n).
The number of buckets in the table (16 by default). Always a power of two; doubles on every resize.
The capacity you ask for in the constructor, e.g. new HashMap<>(64). HashMap rounds it up to the next power of two.
How full the table may get before it grows. Default 0.75: when size > capacity × 0.75, the table doubles.
more: Lower = fewer collisions but more memory. Higher = less memory but longer chains.

short: capacity × load factor. When the number of entries exceeds it, HashMap resizes. 12 for a 16-bucket table.
Doubling the table and moving entries into the new, larger array.
more: Java 8+ does not recompute any hash: each node either keeps its index or moves by exactly the old capacity.

short: Converting a long chain in one bucket into a red-black tree, so lookups drop from O(n) to O(log n).
more: Happens when a bucket reaches 9 nodes AND the table has at least 64 buckets. With fewer buckets HashMap resizes instead.

short: Turning a tree bucket back into a plain linked list when it has shrunk to 6 nodes or fewer.
A bucket that holds its nodes as a red-black tree (TreeNode objects) instead of a linked list.
more: TreeNodes are roughly twice as big as plain nodes, which is why HashMap only uses them for long chains.

short: A self-balancing binary search tree. Guarantees search, insert and delete in O(log n).
more: TreeMap is built on the same structure.

short: A tree where every node has at most two children, smaller keys on the left and larger on the right. Search takes one comparison per level.
The last-resort ordering inside a tree bin when hashes are equal and keys are not Comparable: class name, then identity hash code.
more: It keeps the tree consistent but cannot help lookups, which must then check both subtrees.

short: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 … Exactly one bit set in binary, which makes (n - 1) a mask of all ones.
more: That is why a bitwise AND can replace the slower modulo.

short: The & operator: each result bit is 1 only if both input bits are 1. With a mask like 0b1111 it keeps just the low bits.
The ^ operator: each result bit is 1 when the two input bits differ.
Unsigned right shift. h >>> 16 moves the top 16 bits down to the bottom and fills with zeros, even for negative numbers.
A number whose 1-bits select which bits of another number to keep when combined with &.
more: For capacity 16 the mask is 15 = 0b1111, so only the lowest 4 bits of the hash are used.

short: The % operator, the remainder after division. For a power-of-two n and non-negative h, h % n equals h & (n - 1) but the AND is faster and never negative.
HashMap's step h ^ (h >>> 16): it mixes the high 16 bits of the hash into the low 16 bits.
more: Only the low bits pick the bucket in a small table, so without this, hashes that differ only in high bits would all collide.

short: Constant time: the work does not grow with the number of entries.
Linear time: the work grows in step with the number of entries, e.g. walking a whole chain.
Logarithmic time: doubling the entries adds only one more step, as in a balanced tree.
Averaged over many operations. One resize is expensive, but spread over all the puts that led to it, the cost per put is still O(1).
An object whose fields can never change after construction (String, Integer, records). Ideal as map keys.
An object whose fields can change after construction. If a key's fields feed hashCode() and you change them, the map can no longer find it.
The default Object.hashCode(): a number tied to the object's identity, not its contents. Two equal-looking objects get different ones.
more: Not the memory address in modern JVMs; usually a generated pseudo-random number stored in the object header.

short: An interface with compareTo() that defines a natural order. Tree bins use it, when available, to order keys that share a hash.
more: String and Integer implement it.

short: A helper that combines several fields into one hash code (31 × previous + next field). Convenient for hashCode() implementations.
more: Allocates a varargs array, so hand-write the maths in very hot code.

short: A Java 16+ class for plain immutable data. The compiler generates equals(), hashCode() and toString() from the components.
more: Good map keys.

short: Automatic wrapping of a primitive such as int into its object type Integer, needed because maps hold objects.
Safe to use from several threads at once without corrupting data.
more: HashMap is not thread-safe.

short: A bug where the result depends on the unlucky timing of two threads touching the same data.
Two threads read the same value, both change it, and one change silently overwrites the other.
Java keyword that lets only one thread at a time run a block of code or method on a given lock.
A mechanism that lets only one thread at a time enter a critical section.
Compare-and-swap: a CPU instruction that updates a value only if it still holds the expected old value. Basis of lock-free algorithms.
more: ConcurrentHashMap uses it to put the first node into an empty bucket.

short: A thread-safe hash map. Java 8+: CAS for empty buckets, a lock on the first node of a bucket otherwise. No null keys or values.
more: Reads are lock-free; writes to different buckets run in parallel.

short: A legacy thread-safe map from Java 1.0. Every method is synchronized on one lock, and null keys/values are not allowed.
more: Avoid in new code.

short: Wraps any map so that every method takes a single lock. Thread-safe but a bottleneck under contention; iteration still needs manual locking.
An iterator that throws ConcurrentModificationException as soon as it notices the map was changed behind its back.
more: Best-effort only: it is a bug detector, not a guarantee.

short: Thrown by fail-fast iterators when the collection is structurally modified during iteration (other than via the iterator's own remove).
A counter HashMap increments on every structural change. Iterators remember it and compare it on each step to detect interference.
An object that walks through a collection one element at a time.
A HashMap that also keeps a doubly linked list through its entries, so iteration follows insertion order (or access order).
more: With accessOrder = true and removeEldestEntry it makes a simple LRU cache.

short: A map kept sorted by key, implemented as a red-black tree. O(log n) operations, no hashing.
more: Needs Comparable keys or a Comparator.

short: A set backed by a HashMap: the elements are the keys, and every value is the same dummy object.
A map that compares keys with == and System.identityHashCode instead of equals/hashCode. Used for object-graph work.
A map whose keys are held weakly: when nothing else references a key, the entry disappears.
A very compact map for enum keys, backed by an array indexed by the enum's ordinal.
Least-recently-used cache: when full, it evicts the entry that has gone unused the longest.
Map method that computes and stores a value only when the key is missing. The mapping function must not modify the same map.
A loop that never ends. In Java 7, concurrent resizes could turn a chain into a circle so a get() spun forever.
Memory that is still referenced and so can never be garbage-collected, though the program no longer uses it.
more: A mutated key can leave an unreachable-but-referenced entry in a map.

short: The JVM's automatic freeing of objects that nothing references any more.
The JVM memory area, shared by all threads, where every object and array lives until the garbage collector frees it.
more: Sized with -Xms and -Xmx. The string pool is part of it.

short: HashMap allows one null key; its hash is defined as 0, so it always lives in bucket 0.
Creating something only when first needed. HashMap allocates its table on the first put, not in the constructor.
Choosing the initial capacity from the expected number of entries, so the map never has to resize while filling.
more: Capacity needed = expected entries ÷ 0.75, rounded up.

short: A statistical model for how many random items land in one slot. The JDK authors used it to show that 8 nodes in a bucket is vanishingly rare with decent hash codes.
more: Chance of 8 nodes in one bucket is about 0.00000006.

short: Keys spread evenly across all buckets, which is what a good hash function aims for.
If you put more pigeons than holes, some hole must hold two. Here: more possible keys than buckets means collisions are certain.
A denial-of-service attack where someone sends many keys with the same hash code to force long chains and slow the server.
more: Tree bins (Java 8+) limit the damage to O(log n) when keys are Comparable.

short: An attack that makes a service too slow or busy to use.
One key-value pair of a Map, as seen through iteration. HashMap's Node implements it.
Java Development Kit: the compiler, tools and the standard library, including java.util.HashMap.
Java Virtual Machine, the runtime that executes Java bytecode.
A field modifier that makes writes visible to all threads immediately.
A counter that spreads updates over several cells to avoid contention. ConcurrentHashMap's size counter works the same way.
Whether one thread can see the changes made by another. Without synchronization it may not.
JDK Enhancement Proposal: the numbered document that describes one change to the JDK.
more: Read any of them at openjdk.org/jeps/<number>. Each one records the motivation, design and the release it targets.

short: Java Specification Request: a standard defined through the Java Community Process.
more: Older than JEPs for big API changes, for example JSR 335 for lambdas and JSR 310 for java.time.

short: Long-term support: a release the vendor keeps patching for years. Java LTS versions are 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25.
more: Other releases get about six months of updates, so most production systems stay on LTS versions.

short: A finished design shipped for feedback. Needs --enable-preview and may change in the next release.
more: Code compiled with preview features only runs on the exact same Java version.

short: An API shipped in a jdk.incubator.* module that you must add explicitly. It may change or vanish.
more: The Vector API has incubated since Java 16.

short: A JVM feature behind -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions that is not yet production-ready.
more: ZGC was experimental in Java 11 to 14, Shenandoah in 12 to 14.

short: Java Platform Module System (Java 9): modules declare what they require and export in module-info.java.
more: It made the JDK itself modular and enabled strong encapsulation and jlink runtime images.

short: An anonymous function written as (args) -> body. It implements a functional interface.
more: Added in Java 8 (JSR 335), compiled using invokedynamic.

short: An interface with exactly one abstract method, so a lambda or method reference can implement it.
more: Examples: Runnable, Comparator, Function, Predicate.

short: Java 8 library for declarative pipelines over collections: filter, map, collect.
more: Streams are lazy and can run in parallel.

short: An interface method with a body (Java 8), so interfaces can gain methods without breaking implementers.
more: Allowed Collection.stream() and Map.computeIfAbsent() to be added to old interfaces.

short: Native-memory area holding class metadata. Replaced PermGen in Java 8.
more: Limit it with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize. It grows on demand.

short: The fixed-size heap region that held class metadata before Java 8 (OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space).
more: Interned strings left it in Java 7; the rest went to Metaspace in Java 8 (JEP 122).

short: The region-based garbage collector aiming for predictable pauses. Default since Java 9.
more: Supported in 7u4, default on server machines in 9, default everywhere in Java 27.

short: A low-latency garbage collector doing nearly all work concurrently, with millisecond pauses.
more: Experimental in 11, production in 15, generational in 21, generational by default in 23.

short: A low-pause garbage collector from Red Hat that compacts concurrently.
more: Experimental in 12, production in 15, generational mode product in 25.

short: Concurrent Mark Sweep: an older low-pause collector, deprecated in 9 and removed in 14.
more: G1 replaced it for most uses.

short: A garbage collector that allocates but never reclaims memory (Java 11).
more: Used for performance tests and very short-lived programs.

short: The just-in-time compiler that turns hot bytecode into machine code while the program runs.
more: HotSpot has two: C1 (fast) and C2 (optimising).

short: The standard Oracle/OpenJDK virtual machine, with adaptive JIT compilation. Default since Java 1.3.
The platform-independent instruction set that javac produces and the JVM runs.
more: Stored in .class files.

short: A JVM instruction (Java 7) for linking calls at run time.
more: Powers lambdas, string concatenation and dynamic languages on the JVM.

short: New I/O: buffers, channels and selectors (Java 1.4), and the Path/Files API (NIO.2, Java 7).
Java 5 feature letting classes and methods take type parameters, such as List<String>.
more: Implemented by type erasure.

short: The compiler removes generic type arguments after checking, so List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class at run time.
more: Kept old code compatible with generics.

short: Metadata attached to code with @, such as @Override. Readable by tools and frameworks (Java 5).
A fixed set of named constants, which can have fields and methods (Java 5).
A method parameter written Type... that accepts any number of arguments (Java 5).
try (var r = open()) { ... } closes AutoCloseable resources automatically (Java 7).
Writing <> so the compiler infers type arguments: new ArrayList<>() (Java 7).
A class or interface that lists exactly which classes may extend it. Final in Java 17.
more: Lets the compiler check that a switch covers every case.

short: Testing a value against a shape and extracting parts in one step: instanceof, switch and record patterns.
more: Delivered over Java 14 to 21.

short: A lightweight thread managed by the JVM rather than the OS. Final in Java 21 (Project Loom).
more: You can run millions of them.

short: A normal Java thread backed one-to-one by an operating-system thread.
Treating a group of concurrent tasks as one unit with one lifetime. Still preview through Java 27.
Immutable data shared with child tasks for a bounded time; the modern alternative to ThreadLocal. Final in Java 25.
OpenJDK project for smaller, more productive language features such as var, records and pattern matching.
OpenJDK project for lightweight concurrency: virtual threads, structured concurrency, scoped values.
OpenJDK project connecting Java to native code and data: Foreign Function and Memory API, Vector API.
OpenJDK project adding value types for flatter, faster memory layouts. Still in progress.
OpenJDK project improving startup and warm-up time, using ahead-of-time caches.
OpenJDK project shrinking object headers from 12 bytes to 8.
The Java 7 project for small language changes: diamond, try-with-resources, multi-catch.
Foreign Function and Memory API: safe calls to native code and off-heap memory. Final in Java 22.
more: Replaces JNI.

short: The older, awkward way to call C/C++ code from Java.
more: Java 24 starts warning about its use.

short: An API for SIMD vector computations. Incubating since Java 16.
Standard API for reading and writing .class files. Final in Java 24.
Custom intermediate operations for streams. Final in Java 24.
The old in-JVM sandbox for untrusted code. Deprecated for removal in 17, permanently disabled in 24.
A small Java program embedded in a web page, from the Java 1.0 era. API removed in Java 26.
A modern UI toolkit bundled with Java 8 to 10, now separate as OpenJFX.
Class-data sharing: a pre-parsed archive of classes mapped at startup to start faster and save memory.
Class loading, linking and profile data recorded in one run and reused in the next to speed up startup (Project Leyden).
Java Flight Recorder: low-overhead event recording built into the JVM. Open-sourced in Java 11.
The JavaScript engine in the JDK from Java 8, deprecated in 11 and removed in 15.
An old distributed-object standard. Removed from the JDK in Java 11.
The successor to Java EE, run by the Eclipse Foundation. Since version 9 packages are jakarta.* instead of javax.*.
more: Spring Boot 3 uses it.

short: A phase in which all application threads are paused so the garbage collector can work.
A collector that separates young, short-lived objects from old ones, because most objects die young.
A smaller object header (8 bytes instead of 12) from Project Lilliput: less heap, better cache use.
more: Product in 25, default in 27.

short: Java 21 interfaces for collections with a defined order, adding getFirst(), getLast() and reversed().
A multi-line string in triple quotes that keeps its line breaks. Final in Java 15.
The open-source reference implementation of Java. Oracle, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto and others build from it.
The Java compiler. It turns .java source into .class bytecode.
A tool that builds a trimmed runtime containing only the modules an application needs (Java 9).
The Java REPL for trying code interactively (Java 9).
A container that holds a value or nothing, to avoid returning null (Java 8).
A Future you can compose and chain without blocking (Java 8).
A framework for splitting work into subtasks run on a work-stealing pool (Java 7).
The rules for when one thread is guaranteed to see another thread's writes. Rewritten in Java 5 (JSR 133).
A class like Integer or Optional whose instances should be treated as interchangeable values, not locked on or compared by identity.
A class generated at run time that cannot be used directly by other classes (Java 15), used by lambdas and frameworks.
A G1 option that shares the backing array of equal strings to save heap.
NullPointerException messages that name the exact variable or call that was null (Java 14).
Per-thread memory holding one frame per method call: local variables, parameters and partial results.
more: Freed automatically when a method returns. Sized with -Xss.

short: The block of the stack created for one method call: its local variables, an operand stack and bookkeeping. Popped when the method returns.
Scratch space inside a stack frame where the JVM evaluates expressions.
A table inside the heap that holds one String object per distinct literal, so equal literals share an object.
more: Since Java 7 it lives in the heap, so unused strings can be collected.

short: String.intern() returns the pooled String with the same characters, adding it to the pool if needed.
The JVM area for class metadata and method bytecode. In HotSpot it is the permanent generation (before Java 8) or Metaspace (Java 8 onwards).
Per-class table of literals and symbolic references that the JVM resolves while running.
The object that finds and loads a class. Classes are unloaded only when their class loader is unreachable.
Thread-local allocation buffer: a private slice of eden so a thread can allocate objects with a simple pointer bump and no lock.
The part of the young generation where new objects are first allocated.
Two small young-generation areas used alternately to hold objects that survived a collection but are not yet old enough to be promoted.
The part of the heap for new objects (eden plus survivor spaces), collected often and cheaply.
more: Most objects die here.

short: The part of the heap for long-lived objects promoted from the young generation. Collected less often.
A starting point for reachability: local variables on thread stacks, static fields, live threads and JNI references.
more: An object is kept only if it can be reached from a root.

short: An object is reachable if some chain of references leads to it from a GC root. Unreachable objects can be collected.
A JIT analysis that checks whether an object can be seen outside its method or thread. If not, the allocation and locks can be removed.
Thrown when a thread's stack is full, almost always from unbounded recursion.
Thrown when a memory area is exhausted. The message names the area: Java heap space, Metaspace, Direct buffer memory and so on.
Storing object references in 4 bytes instead of 8 on a 64-bit JVM, possible for heaps up to about 32 GB.
The bookkeeping at the start of every object: a mark word (hash code, lock and GC state) and a class pointer. 12 bytes on 64-bit HotSpot with compressed pointers.
Native memory allocated outside the Java heap, for example by ByteBuffer.allocateDirect. Used to avoid copies during I/O.
JVM flag that sets the maximum heap size.
more: Default: a quarter of the machine or container memory.

short: JVM flag that sets the initial heap size.
JVM flag that sets the stack size of each thread.
The Java Memory Model guarantee: if action A happens-before action B, then A's effects are visible to B and A appears to run first.
more: Created by program order, lock/unlock, volatile write/read, Thread.start() and join().

short: Two threads access the same variable, at least one writes, and nothing orders them (no happens-before). The outcome is not guaranteed.
The compiler and the CPU may run independent operations in a different order than written, as long as one thread cannot tell. Other threads can.
An operation that happens entirely or not at all, with no other thread seeing it half done.
more: count++ is not atomic.

short: Making an object visible to other threads only after it is fully constructed, using volatile, a lock, a final field or a thread-safe hand-off.
Per-thread register holding the address of the JVM instruction currently being run.
The basic collection method: mark everything reachable from the roots, then reclaim the unmarked objects.
Sliding live objects together to remove gaps, so memory stays in one big free block and allocation is a pointer bump.
more: Without it the heap fragments: plenty of free space, but no hole big enough.

short: Collecting by copying the live objects to a new area and discarding the old one. Cost depends on live data, not on garbage.
more: Used for the young generation and by G1 evacuation pauses.

short: The observation that most objects die young, which is why heaps are split into young and old generations.
A collection of only the young generation. Frequent and short.
A collection of the whole heap. The most expensive kind of collection; many of them in a log signal trouble.
A G1 collection that cleans young regions plus the old regions with the most garbage.
Moving an object from the young to the old generation after it survives enough collections.
The number of young collections an object must survive before it is promoted. Adaptive, at most 15.
A point where the JVM can stop a thread safely, so the collector can read or move objects. All threads are brought to one for a stop-the-world pause.
A small piece of code the JIT adds after every reference store, so the collector learns about changed references (for example to mark a card dirty).
A check on every reference load, used by ZGC to fix up references so objects can be moved while the program runs.
A table marking which parts of the old generation changed, so a young collection scans only those instead of the whole old generation.
In G1, an object at least half a region in size. It gets its own regions and is expensive to churn.
Snapshot-at-the-beginning: concurrent marking that treats the object graph as it was when marking started, recording overwritten references with a barrier.
ZGC stores metadata bits inside each 64-bit reference so the collector and load barriers know the object's state.
A single-threaded, stop-the-world collector with the smallest footprint. Chosen automatically on tiny machines.
A stop-the-world collector that uses many threads, tuned for maximum throughput. Default up to Java 8.
An ordinary reference: the object cannot be collected while it is reachable through it.
A reference cleared only when the JVM is short of memory. Suits memory-sensitive caches.
A reference that does not keep its target alive: it is cleared at the next collection once nothing else references the object.
more: WeakHashMap uses them for its keys.

short: A reference used only to learn that an object has been collected, so cleanup can run. get() always returns null.
The old Object.finalize() cleanup hook. Slow and unreliable; deprecated for removal in Java 18.
more: Use try-with-resources or Cleaner instead.

short: java.lang.ref.Cleaner: registers a cleanup action to run after an object becomes unreachable. A safety net, not a replacement for closing resources.
How fast the program creates new objects, usually in MB per second. The main driver of young collection frequency.
How long the application is frozen during a stop-the-world collection. Watch the maximum and 99th percentile.
The collector's record of each collection: type, cause, heap before and after, and pause time. Enabled with -Xlog:gc.
A heap-dump view showing which objects keep the most memory alive. The first place to look for a leak.
The G1 pause-time goal, 200 ms by default. G1 adjusts how much it collects to try to stay within it.
Threads each hold a lock and wait for one held by another, so none can ever continue.
more: Needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Prevent it with a global lock order.

short: Threads are not blocked but keep reacting to each other and make no progress.
A thread never gets the lock or CPU time it needs because others always win.
The lock built into every Java object, taken by synchronized. Reentrant: the owner can take it again.
A lock that the thread already holding it can acquire again without blocking itself.
more: Both synchronized and ReentrantLock are reentrant.

short: A fixed set of reusable threads that take tasks from a queue, instead of creating a thread per task.
The configurable thread pool: core size, maximum size, work queue, keep-alive and rejection policy.
more: It queues tasks before growing beyond the core size.

short: What a full thread pool does with a new task: abort (throw), run it on the caller, discard it or discard the oldest.
Separating resources (for example thread pools) so a failure or slowness in one part cannot exhaust everything else.
Idle worker threads take tasks from the queues of busy workers, so all cores stay busy. Used by ForkJoinPool.
The work-stealing thread pool behind Fork/Join, parallel streams and default CompletableFuture tasks.
more: The shared common pool has about one thread fewer than the number of cores.

short: A queue whose put() blocks when full and take() blocks when empty. The standard tool for producer-consumer.
Slowing down a producer when the consumer cannot keep up, for example by blocking on a full bounded queue.
A thread returning from wait() without being notified. That is why wait() must be called in a while loop.
A variable with a separate value for each thread. Clear it with remove() on pooled threads to avoid leaks.
more: Scoped values replace it from Java 25.

short: The platform thread on which a virtual thread runs while it is mounted.
A virtual thread that cannot unmount while blocked (inside synchronized before Java 24, or in native code), so it holds its carrier thread.
Lets threads wait until a count of events reaches zero. Single-use.
Makes a fixed number of threads wait for each other at a point, then lets them all continue. Reusable.
Hands out a fixed number of permits to limit how many threads use a resource at once.
An explicit lock with tryLock, timeouts, interruptible locking, fairness and conditions. Always unlock in finally.
A lock with optimistic reads that skip locking and validate afterwards. Not reentrant (Java 8).
A variable updated atomically using compare-and-swap, without locks.
A value changes from A to B and back to A, so a compare-and-swap cannot tell anything changed. Fixed with a version stamp.
Thrown by blocking methods when the thread was interrupted. Rethrow it or restore the flag; never swallow it.
A background thread that does not stop the JVM from exiting. The JVM exits when only daemon threads remain.
A snapshot of every thread with its state and stack, taken with jcmd Thread.print or jstack. The first tool for a hang or deadlock.
An iterator or size that reflects some state of a concurrent collection during the call, not a frozen snapshot. It never throws ConcurrentModificationException.
Keeping data inside a single thread so it never needs locking: locals, ThreadLocal or a single-thread executor.
Many threads competing for the same lock or atomic variable, so most of them wait or retry.
A race where code checks a condition and then acts on it, but another thread changes the condition in between.
more: Fix with an atomic method such as putIfAbsent.

short: A pattern where some threads put work on a queue and others take it off, decoupling their speeds.
Bundling data with the methods that act on it and hiding the internals, so the object can protect its own rules.
more: Not the same as having getters and setters for every field.

short: Exposing what something does and hiding how, so callers depend on a simple contract instead of details.
A subclass reusing and extending a superclass with extends: an is-a relationship.
more: The tightest coupling between classes; use it only when the subclass truly is a kind of the parent.

short: One call, different behaviour depending on the object: overriding (decided at run time) and overloading (decided at compile time).
A subclass replacing an inherited method with the same signature. Which version runs is decided at run time by the actual class.
Several methods with the same name and different parameter lists. The compiler chooses from the declared argument types.
Choosing which overridden method to run from the actual class of the object when the call executes.
more: HotSpot uses a vtable and often inlines the call.

short: The per-class table of virtual methods the JVM uses to find an overriding method with one lookup.
A class that cannot be instantiated and may hold state, constructors and unimplemented abstract methods for subclasses to fill in. A class can extend only one.
Building a class from other objects it holds and delegates to (has-a), instead of inheriting from them.
more: Usually preferred over inheritance.

short: An object handing a job to another object it holds, instead of doing it itself or inheriting it.
A change to a superclass that looks safe but breaks its subclasses, because they depend on its implementation.
Five design principles: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion.
A subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is expected without surprising the caller.
more: Classic violation: Square extends Rectangle.

short: Passing an object its collaborators from outside (usually through the constructor) instead of creating them inside.
High-level code depends on abstractions (interfaces), not on concrete low-level classes.
A framework controls the flow and wires your objects together, instead of your code doing it. Spring is an IoC container.
How much one module depends on another. Lower is better.
How closely related the things inside one class are. Higher is better.
Talk to your direct collaborators, not to their internals: order.customer().address().city() is a smell.
Tell an object to do something instead of pulling its data out and deciding for it.
Entities that only have getters and setters, with all the rules in separate service classes. Procedural code in an OO disguise.
A class that knows and does too much. A sign that it has many reasons to change.
An overriding method returning a subtype of the parent method's return type.
Copying a mutable argument or result so the caller cannot change your object's internal state.
An interface with no methods that only tags a class, such as Serializable.
A hidden method the compiler generates so covariant returns and generics still dispatch correctly at run time.
A non-static nested class. Holds a hidden reference to its enclosing instance, which can cause memory leaks.
A class declared and instantiated in one expression, without a name.
A design pattern: pick an algorithm at run time behind an interface (Comparator, shipping policies).
A class with exactly one instance. In Java the safest forms are an enum and the holder idiom.
A named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem: Strategy, Factory, Builder, Observer and so on.
Treating an object as its supertype (upcast, always safe) or back as a subtype (downcast, checked at run time).
A class should have one reason to change, that is, answer to one actor.
Add new behaviour by adding code, not by editing existing tested code.
Clients should not depend on methods they do not use: prefer several small interfaces to one big one.
Don't repeat yourself: each piece of knowledge lives in one place.
more: About duplicated knowledge, not just similar-looking text.

short: Keep it simple: choose the simplest design that works.
You aren't gonna need it: do not build for needs you only imagine.
Duplicate once; generalise the third time, when you can see what really varies.
The "Gang of Four": authors of the 1994 Design Patterns book that describes 23 patterns.
A common solution that looks reasonable but causes more problems than it solves.
A static method that creates or returns instances, with a name and freedom to cache or return a subtype: List.of, Integer.valueOf.
A pattern for creating objects without naming the concrete class. An abstract factory creates families of related objects.
Constructing a complex object step by step through a fluent API, finishing with build().
Making one interface look like another that the client expects, so incompatible classes work together.
Adding behaviour by wrapping an object that has the same interface. java.io readers and streams are decorators.
A stand-in with the same interface that controls access to another object. Spring AOP and Hibernate lazy loading use proxies.
One simple interface in front of a complicated subsystem.
A subject notifies any number of subscribers when something happens, without knowing who they are.
A base class fixes the skeleton of an algorithm and subclasses fill in some steps.
Turning a request into an object so it can be queued, logged, retried or undone. Runnable is a command.
An object changes behaviour as its state changes, replacing switches on a status field.
A request passes along ordered handlers until one handles it. Servlet filters and the Spring Security filter chain.
Treating single objects and groups of objects uniformly, for tree structures.
Sharing identical immutable objects to save memory, like the Integer cache and the string pool.
Choosing a method from the run-time types of two objects. The Visitor pattern uses it.
A plain object shaped for the wire, so internal entities do not leak through an API.
An object that encapsulates data access for one entity or table.
A collection-like interface for loading and saving aggregates, hiding the persistence details. Spring Data JpaRepository.
The entry-point object of a cluster of related objects, responsible for enforcing their invariants (domain-driven design).
A global registry classes call to look up dependencies. Hides what a class needs; prefer dependency injection.
Behaviour needed in many places, such as logging, security and transactions, that is separated out with filters, proxies or aspects.
Aspect-oriented programming: adding cross-cutting behaviour around methods without editing them. Spring implements it with proxies.
A proxy class generated at run time: JDK proxies implement interfaces; CGLIB or ByteBuddy generate a subclass.
A class with many constructors adding one optional parameter each, which become unreadable. A Builder is the usual fix.
